## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="w10-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Decisions</dt><dd>What the model chooses: here the two gas plants' outputs, spilled wind and sun, and unserved demand.</dd>
<dt>Goal</dt><dd>What it makes as small as possible: the running cost.</dd>
<dt>Rules</dt><dd>What every plan must obey: balance, plant sizes, the ramp limit, a CO₂ cap.</dd>
<dt>Given</dt><dd>Data the model takes as it is: demand, weather, costs.</dd>
<dt>Four outcomes</dt><dd>One best corner, a tie along an edge, infeasible (no plan meets every rule) or unbounded (a rule is missing).</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Why the best plan sits at a corner</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

1. The cost line $40x + 100y = C$ keeps its slope as $C$ changes: lowering $C$ slides it in parallel.
2. The last point it touches in the shaded [feasible region]{.lx-term term="feasible-region"} is a corner, or a whole edge that lies along the line (a tie).
3. So for this two-plant model, where neither output can go below zero, whenever a best plan exists at least one best plan sits at a corner.

| Case | Best corner | Gas cost for the hour |
|---|---|---|
| 19:00 as given (145 MW of gas) | $x = 145$, $y = 0$ (53.65 t of CO₂) | \$5,800 |
| 200 MW of gas | $x = 150$, $y = 50$ | \$11,000 |

The fixed-output plant adds a constant \$1,000 for the hour (100 MW × \$10/MWh), so 19:00 costs \$6,800 in all. A constant cannot move the best plan, so the chart leaves it out.

[Lesson 11](11-solver.html)'s solver walks from corner to corner in the same way (the [simplex method]{.lx-term term="simplex-method"}).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The hour as a solver reads it</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A solver reads the same four parts, written as numbers. For 19:00, in one line:

$$
\min\ 40x + 100y \quad \text{subject to} \quad x + y \ge 145,\ \ x \le 150,\ \ y \le 100,\ \ 0.37x + 0.55y \le 100,\ \ x, y \ge 0.
$$

- **Decisions:** $x$ and $y$, in MW for the hour.
- **Goal:** the gas cost in dollars, one coefficient per decision.
- **Rules:** one row each, with a limit on the right.

Where it goes next:

- [Lesson 11](11-solver.html): the whole day, 96 decisions, handed to the HiGHS solver in your browser.
- [B1](b01-algebra-to-lp.html): rules written as rows of a matrix, step by step.
- [M1](m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html): the same kind of model in Python, in a notebook.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What one hour leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The ramp limit: it couples neighboring hours. This chart leaves out the previous hour's output; <a href="11-solver.html">lesson 11</a> solves all 24 hours together.</li>
<li>Extra gas above 145 MW would be spilled as wind and sun; at 19:00 only 86 MW of them can be, a limit the chart leaves out.</li>
<li>Real costs are rarely exactly equal, but near-ties are common: then small data changes swing the plan between the tied plants.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="w10-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="two" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If two different plans are both best, there are exactly two best plans.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Every plan on the straight segment between them also meets every rule and costs the same, so infinitely many plans tie.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dem" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Demand is one of the decisions in a dispatch model.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Demand is given; the model decides how the plants meet it.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="corner" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “When this lesson's two-plant model has a best plan, at least one best plan sits at a corner of the region.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact, for this model: with both outputs at least zero, its region has corners. The cost line slides in parallel and last touches a corner, or a whole edge that ends at one.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="infeas" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “‘Infeasible’ means the solver failed.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It means the rules contradict each other. Fix the model or its data, not the solver.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="w10">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="var" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which is a decision variable in Prairie Town's dispatch model?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Demand at 19:00</li><li data-value="b">The peaker's output at 19:00</li><li data-value="c">The price of gas</li><li data-value="d">The peaker's CO₂ per MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The peaker's output: the operator chooses it. The other three are given.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="c200" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Gas must supply 200 MW: the combined-cycle costs $40/MWh up to 150 MW, the peaker $100/MWh. What does the cheapest gas plan cost for the hour?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$8,000</li><li data-value="b">$11,000</li><li data-value="c">$20,000</li><li data-value="d">$6,000</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$11,000: 150 MW × $40 + 50 MW × $100. The best corner sits where the combined-cycle's size meets the demand line.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>Grid operators' dispatch models have the same four parts, with many more decisions: every plant, every line, every interval.</p>
<p>Open modeling tools such as <a href="https://docs.pypsa.org/">PyPSA</a> and <a href="https://jump.dev/">JuMP</a> write them in code.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a> (Form EIA-930): the Southwest Power Pool data behind Prairie Town's day.</li>
<li>HiGHS. <a href="https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/">Documentation</a>: the open-source solver that lesson 11 runs in your browser.</li>
<li>JuMP. <a href="https://jump.dev/">Modeling language for mathematical optimization</a> in Julia.</li>
<li>Earlier lessons: <a href="00-grid-operator.html">lesson 0</a> (the day you ran by hand), <a href="08-merit-order.html">lesson 8</a> (the merit order as an optimization).</li>
</ul>
